text:
Chapter Twenty-Two


Arthur’s mind had been racing for hours. He hadn’t heard from Dahlia since the night before, when he’d dashed off a frantic text every hour after he’d returned to Atlantia only to have her finally tell him she was going to shut off her phone if he didn’t stop bugging her. She didn’t realize that it was all replaying in his head, over and over—Maggie collapsing as that bright burst of light struck her palm, Maggie in and out of consciousness as he tried to wake her, Maggie curled in his arms as he raced her back down to the basement.


When he let himself put down the guilt, never for very long, he thought about Maggie’s apartment. It was so lived-in and so Maggie, he’d wanted to sink into the couch beside her and call it home. He shook that thought away before it had a chance to turn into longing.


He tried to distract himself by looking over the notes he’d taken in the Annex, but he could barely read his already messy handwriting as the words swam across the page. He was exhausted. He’d barely slept the night before, but he couldn’t get his body to still. It was in constant movement, with his leg bouncing up and down and his fingers tapping against the ancient, pockmarked wood of his childhood desk.


“Arthur, I can hear you fidgeting from out here,” came his father’s voice, carrying down the short hallway from the living room. “It’s seven in the morning.”


“Sorry, Pop,” he called back, and that strange feeling of time folding in on itself appeared again.


After a moment, he heard the shuffling sounds of Barry getting up from his recliner and walking down the hall. “What are you working on, kiddo?”


Arthur looked up to see his father leaning in the doorway, looking much the same as he’d looked for Arthur’s entire childhood. He wore his park ranger shirt, unbuttoned to reveal an ancient undershirt with holes around the neck, but now his hair was silver gray, and his face had deep lines from too many days in the sun.


Arthur wanted to tell his father everything, but he couldn’t bring himself to share his failures with Barry. The bubbling panic he felt when he thought of the pall, of the way dissolving it and sealing the fissure had evaded him, of the damage he’d caused. The danger he’d put Maggie in corroded everything, caustic and burning.


“It’s just a tricky equation,” he said, as if that could possibly cover everything. If I tell Maggie the truth, the odds of her wanting nothing to do with me are…If I refuse to let Maggie back into the pall, the probability she will go in there herself without me is…If I race back to Maggie’s apartment and confess how I feel, the chance that she will kick me out before I can finish my sentence is…


“Hmm,” Barry replied, his wiry frosted eyebrows knitting together in a furry V. “I’m not sure I’ve ever seen one of your homework problems get you this worked up.” There was a time when that little joke would have felt like a barb, but Arthur had long learned to let it go. “Is there anything I can help you with?”


Arthur was a little ashamed when his first instinct was to scrunch up his nose and dismiss his father, but then he looked down at the journal in his hands. If there was one thing his father knew well, it was the Wilds. “Pop,” he began, and his dad walked into the room, sitting on his old twin bed with the worn quilt Lane had stitched for him in another life. “What do you know about the river confluence in the Wilds?”


Barry took the journal from Arthur’s hands, flipping the ancient pages with a delicate touch. He read the passages Arthur had marked and looked at his son thoughtfully. “More of an annoyance than anything,” Barry said. “Your brother would know better than me, he’s done all the extra wardsmith training, but every ward around the confluence point where the three rivers meet has extra fortifications to account for it. It can get dicey over there sometimes.”


“And Rory would know what these extra fortifications are?”


“He should. Otherwise, what did I pay for all those extra classes for?” Barry grumbled. He turned the page in the journal again. “Oh, now, even I know what this is.” He held the opened journal out to Arthur, tapping a page with a drawing of a vining plant snaking up a tree trunk. “Gloaming creeper,” Barry read. “We’re always looking for more of the stuff. A decoction made out of it can really boost a rune near the confluence, but gods below, is it hard to find.”


Arthur’s mind was suddenly awake, whirring to life. When chalk, paint, or ink was infused with a decoction made from a plant or mineral with known magical properties, it made the spell stronger or could counteract confounding variables. He’d tried plenty of decoctions to improve his dissipation spells—gold to strengthen the bonds of the magic, vervain and yew to block interference coming from the fissure into the next world—but none of them had accounted for the confluence. But if this vine—the gloaming creeper—could help with warding runes around the confluence, it would stand to reason that it would help with their dissipation runes. An antidote of sorts to the havoc the convergence had caused. If they factored the planetary conjunction into the calculation, if Maggie added to the incantation translation…it might all work. “Where does it grow?”


“I can’t get precise with it. I just know it when I see it,” Barry said. “That’s above my pay grade. Rory’s, too. You might want to check in with someone at that school of yours. They might know better.”


Arthur was already pulling up the directory for the botany department as he said a hurried “Thanks, Pop.”


When Arthur looked up from the directory and scrawled Dr. Silva’s name and number on his notepad, Barry had a thoughtful expression on his face. “Why’s your work taking you into the Wilds, Son?”


Arthur had never felt more like a coward. “Just some troublesome spellwork at the school. It’s nothing important.”


Barry looked like he was going to say something, but he just reached out a hand and squeezed Arthur’s shoulder. After a moment he sighed and said, “Well, don’t work too hard. And turn off the lights when you leave.”


“Sure thing, Pop,” Arthur replied. When he heard the recliner creak and groan, Arthur pulled out his phone to the conversation he’d started with Dahlia.




Arthur: Anything?






Dahlia Hawberry, PhD: For the last time, I will message you when she wakes up






Arthur: Sorry, just worried




Dahlia began typing a response and then she stopped, only to start back up again.




Dahlia Hawberry, PhD: I know






Dahlia Hawberry, PhD: I won’t forget, I promise





—


Dahlia finally texted him a few hours later when Maggie rejoined the land of the living, and the vise that had tightened around Arthur’s chest loosened, just by a bit. By then, Arthur had already emailed and received a response from a Hawthorn botanist named Kel Silva, who had agreed to meet with him and Maggie the next day.


All Arthur wanted to do was race to Maggie’s apartment to see for himself that she was feeling better, but he didn’t know how Maggie would feel about the intrusion. He stared at their text conversation for nearly an hour before he settled on the message to send.




Arthur: Hey






Magnolia Linden, PhD: Hi






Arthur: Are you feeling up for more detective work tomorrow?






Magnolia Linden, PhD: Only if you buy me a black trench coat and promise to call me a dame




When Arthur finally saw Maggie again outside Ulmus Hall, he wasn’t sure he remembered how to breathe. She was maybe a little pale, but she looked like she had gotten enough sleep to fight off most of the effects of the pall sickness. She had pulled her auburn hair back, with loose strands falling around her face, and she was wearing a black long-sleeved shirt that showed her shoulders, the swell and dip of her breasts. If Arthur thought he was wound tight with wanting her before, he was mistaken.


He wanted to sweep her into a hug but gave her space instead. He pushed his glasses up and then swept his fingers through his hair, hearing every parent figure in his life say, Stop fidgeting, as he tried to give his hands something else to do.


“I’m happy to see you upright.” He thought about kicking himself immediately. Why did he open his mouth?


But she laughed, a light sound he wanted to bottle for dreary days. “Yeah, me, too,” she said, and there was something different about the way she spoke. Tender, tentative. Something he couldn’t really name. And she looked at him with an intensity that Arthur didn’t know how to read. After a moment, she dropped her gaze and reached into the tote bag she had slung over her shoulders. “I brought this back for you. Thank you for letting me borrow it.” She held his tweed jacket out to him, but he didn’t want to take it. It had been a gift. It had been the one thing Maggie had asked of him that he could do easily.


“Oh, I—” he muttered, stopping before he could say something he would regret. “Why don’t you hold on to it?”


“I couldn’t—”


“It’s fine,” he said, interrupting her. His voice sounded strangely tight even to his ears. She looked at him with an expression that was a little confused and a little curious but slid the jacket back into her bag. “Did the sleeping aid help?”


She nodded, holding on to the straps of the tote bag like they were a lifeline, and he wondered, for the thousandth time, what she was thinking. “A perfectly dreamless sleep.”


“Good.” He looked her over again, searching for something, anything, to indicate she was still feeling the effects of the pall. Satisfied that she really was feeling better, he nodded toward the building in front of them. “Shall we?”


Dr. Silva greeted them at the door to the plant library. She was an older woman with deep brown skin and curls streaked with gray. Her hair was twisted off her neck and secured with a fern-shaped clip, and her skirt was dotted with purple sprigs of vervain.


“Dr. Taliesin and Dr. Linden, welcome to the plant library,” she said warmly.


The plant library was a room with wide, bright windows on two sides and vining plants hanging from the ceiling. The walls were covered in botanical drawings and maps, cases with dried samples lined the edges of the room, and shelves held book after book on the care and cultivation of every plant imaginable. In one corner there was a large pot housing a particularly sinister-looking carnivorous Cape sundew that had grown to an unnatural size. Its stalks of red tentacles dipped in false nectar were the width of a palm, big enough to ensnare a mouse instead of a fly. On the edge of the pot was a name tag: Bruce. Arthur could have spent hours in here, looking at everything.


After encouraging them to look around, Dr. Silva returned to setting up an old projector with ancient slides. The machine whirred to life with several mechanical clicks. Old photographs flashed on the only blank space on the wall, each one showing detailed shots of different plants with their names written in a careful hand in the upper corner. Demon’s fingernails, bane weed, love-in-a-mist. The machine came to a stop when Dr. Silva finally arrived at a slide labeled Gloaming creeper (day).


Maggie walked up to the projection, the blue light illuminating the soft features of her face, full cheeks and that perfect divot in her upper lip that Arthur was desperate to taste again. He shook his head and was shocked out of his stare by Dr. Silva clearing her throat.


“I believe this is what you’re looking for?” the botanist confirmed as Maggie nodded. “There’s only one place you’re going to find a gloaming creeper on the eastern coast—deep in old-growth forests, like the Wilds.” She reached high above her head to a string and pulled down a map of Hawthorn and the surrounding Wilds. She pointed to the three rivers that eventually met at the confluence several miles into the swampy forest. “The vine tends to grow within a few yards of a water source, on the north side of tree trunks. When it’s found near a confluence like this one in the Wilds, it can counteract the effect the confluence might have on spellwork.”


She turned back to the projector. The gloaming creeper vine snaked up the side of a river birch, with wide, almost heart-shaped leaves. “The stem is a deep purple color, more like an aubergine than a mauve,” she explained. “These leaves are variegated, with colors ranging from a deep green to a creamy white, but they can be solid as well.” Dr. Silva clicked the button on the projector, and the next slide appeared, labeled Gloaming creeper (night). “The most notable thing about the vine, besides its otherworldly properties, is that the leaves curl at night.”


Arthur remembered reading about this property in the journal. “Nyctinasty,” he interjected, supplying the word he’d learned to describe this phenomenon.


“Yes, that’s right!” Dr. Silva beamed. Maggie, who was standing on the other side of the botanist, smirked.


“Show-off,” she mouthed across the room, and he couldn’t help his goofy smile.


Arthur stepped forward to examine the projected image of the vine. “Is there anywhere we can buy a prepared decoction of the gloaming creeper? Price wouldn’t be a concern.”


Dr. Silva shook her head. “Unfortunately, gloaming creeper has never been successfully cultivated. Prepared decoctions are very rare and difficult to transport due to its instability after it’s been heated.” She tapped her foot momentarily, looking thoughtfully at Arthur. “My colleague at Dartwood, Dr. Bellinger, has several rare decoctions in her collection. You might be able to check with her to see if she has any advice.”


Arthur stood in front of the Wilds, studying the landscape, shoulder to shoulder with Maggie. “Some explorer certainly had a good time naming these rivers,” she muttered. The Dismal. The Despair. The Dour.


“It is rather ominous, isn’t it,” he said, feeling a little bit breathless about how close they were standing. Memories threatened to surface—of holding her against him as they’d danced on Beltane, as he’d carried her out of the lab when he’d been so worried she might not wake up. He pushed the memories away and turned to Dr. Silva.


“Do you have an idea of the most likely place to find a gloaming creeper between these three rivers?”


Dr. Silva arched her brows. “If you were going to venture into the Wilds—which I am not recommending, to be clear—I would suggest starting at the Dismal. This part of the Wilds is drier, before you get down into swampier lowlands. You’re going to find sassafras, maybe some white cedar trees. River birches are less common but still a possibility. If the plain has flooded recently, the gloaming creeper could have been washed out, so I would start as far upland as you can. But again, I don’t think I can recommend, in good conscience, that you enter the Wilds. Especially not now.”


“Understood. I don’t think it’s going to be a problem,” Maggie said, but Arthur wasn’t so sure that was the case. Based on everything Dr. Silva explained, there didn’t seem to be another option.


Dr. Silva shuddered. “I’ve always enjoyed living by the Wilds. It’s always felt safe, even with the occasional ghoul or banshee sighting, but this pall has changed things. I’ve been too nervous, even just going from Ulmus Hall to my house.”


Familiar guilt curled in Arthur’s gut. It paralyzed him until he didn’t know what he could say, but then Maggie was offering Dr. Silva reassurance.


“Have you refreshed your ward runes lately?” Maggie asked her, and she responded she just hadn’t had the time. Before Maggie spoke again, she reached over and rested a hand on Arthur’s arm. “Dr. Taliesin and I can come by and take a look for you.”


“Oh, I couldn’t ask you to do that,” Dr. Silva said with a wave of her hand. “You’re both so busy.”


“We would be happy to,” Arthur said, trying not to stare at Maggie’s hand on his arm. Like they were a unit. “It’s the least we can do after your help today.” Maggie’s hand slipped down, her fingers trailing along his elbow before returning to her side.


“That’s very generous of you both. If you mean it, I’ll send an email with my address, and you can come by anytime.” Dr. Silva checked her watch. “I’m so sorry, I have another appointment in the greenhouses in about fifteen minutes. If you need anything else, you can find me there until later this afternoon. Feel free to use the plant library for your research as long as you need. And if you’re going to stay past two, could you give Bruce his lunch?”


Maggie eyed the plant in the corner warily, probably wondering as Arthur was what such a monstrous plant could eat. “Of course,” Arthur said. “We’ll take care of the little guy.”


Alone, Arthur and Maggie split off, looking around the expansive library. Arthur paused in front of the map of the Wilds. The longer he stared at the route the Dismal took in the Wilds—a looping, winding creek that grew in size until it met up with the Dour and the Despair—the more certain he became. Maggie wasn’t going to like it. He sighed.


“Everything okay?” Maggie was back by his side, and he startled as her fingers grazed his elbow again, a look of concern on her face. He looked down at her hand, and she pulled it back like she hadn’t meant to do it at all. Was she touching him more? It felt like something had shifted since they went into the pall together, since he’d carried her out of it. Tell her, came the part of his brain that talked sense, but he ignored it. Again.


Instead, he said, “I hope you like camping.”


Maggie’s face fell, and she looked over at the map he’d been examining. “I hope you don’t mean what I think you mean.” He grimaced. “What about Dartwood? Maybe they have some of the decoction ready.”


Arthur shook his head. “Even if they do, and that’s a big if, it would take too long to get here, and that’s if they’re willing to part with their rare decoction. It would be easier if it was for sale,” he went on, more to himself than Maggie.


“Fine, then we go into the Wilds.” She shuddered. “But what is this about camping? We walk in, we grab the vine, and we go. No tents or sleeping bags necessary.”


Arthur pointed to the Dismal with one finger and the edge of the Wilds with the other. He drew his two fingers together. “Even if we enter at the northernmost point, that’s still a miles-long round trip through dense forest. There’s a path, but the deeper we get, the less well it’s maintained. Even if we rush, even if we find the gloaming creeper right away, we still probably couldn’t do it in one day.”


Maggie crossed her arms. “I did not sign up to camp in the Wilds.”


“It could be fun?”


“I thought you were oh so concerned about my well-being, and you want me to camp in that ghoul-infested hellhole?”


There was something about this Maggie, the one who didn’t give a shit what he thought, that Arthur couldn’t get enough of. He wanted to get a rise out of her, so he smirked. “It’s not as bad as all that.”


“Do you know what’s in there?” she practically shrieked.


“I promise,” he said dryly, “I am very familiar with the flora and fauna of the Wilds.”


“The flora and fauna,” she mimicked. “Well, that sounds downright pleasant. Charming, even. But that forest is nothing but ghoul nests and banshee hideaways.”


“If you take proper precautions, the Wilds are very safe.” Arthur glanced up from the map. His eyes met Maggie’s, and her expression softened as they looked at each other, but when she swallowed, her jaw tightened. “Do you trust me?” he asked her.


He wondered what was running through her mind. He had been reckless with her safety before, and they were here because of his bad decisions. He didn’t blame her for being frightened, for hesitating to put any trust in him when he’d let her down again and again. But fantasmia were predictable. The Wilds were familiar. This was something he was confident he could do.


Before he could reconsider, he reached up and brushed an out-of-place strand of her hair back, pulling his fingers away before they could linger. “I won’t let anything happen to you this time,” he said quietly, stopping short of making a promise he couldn’t keep.


Something like hope bloomed in his chest when she said slowly, “Okay.” She brushed back the same strand of hair. “I trust you.”

facts.fact: Atlantia 失眠夜：每小时狂轰 Dahlia；脑内循环她倒在光珠下/时昏时醒/抱她冲下地下室。
facts.anchor: replaying in his head, over and over

facts.fact: 概率自白：说真相她可能不理他；不让她进 pall 她会自己去；冲去表白她可能没听完就赶人——三条 odds 全没写完。
facts.anchor: the odds of her wanting nothing to do with me

facts.fact: 父子情报：三河交汇点周围每道 ward 都有 extra fortifications；Rory 受过加训更懂。
Gloaming creeper：藤本攀河桦，煎剂增幅交汇点附近符文——难找得很；从未成功栽培。
解法三变量：植物（地）+计算（他）+译文（她）——把行星连珠算进计算也许全盘皆活。
父亲体贴：看穿不说破，捏肩留一句关灯——别太拼。
还外套交锋：她要还、他让她留着（It had been a gift）；她困惑又好奇。
facts.anchor: Why don’t you hold on to it?

facts.fact: 植物馆：Bruce（巨型 Cape sundew）；幻灯片 day/night 两页——叶夜卷（Nyctinasty）、紫茎 variegated 叶。
三河命名：惨淡/绝望/阴郁——采摘路线沿 Dismal 上行；Silva 以良心不推荐进 Wilds。
facts.anchor: The Dismal. The Despair. The Dour.

facts.fact: 她的手搭上他的手臂许诺帮 Silva 查符文——like they were a unit；指尖沿肘滑下。
野营谈判+I trust you：北端进也要 miles-long 往返；他拨正她一缕乱发「这次我不会让任何事发生在你身上」——话到承诺前停住；她拂回同一缕发：Okay. I trust you.。
facts.anchor: I won’t let anything happen to you this time
